summary.text: Partial fraction decomposition expresses a fraction of two polynomials as a sum of a polynomial, possibly zero, and one or several fractions with simpler denominators.
It matters because it provides algorithms for computing antiderivatives, Taylor series expansions, inverse Z-transforms and inverse Laplace transforms of rational functions.
If the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's, you first divide using polynomial long division, then decompose the leftover fraction.

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: Independently by Johann Bernoulli and Gottfried Leibniz in 1702

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: Antiderivatives, Taylor series, inverse Z- and Laplace transforms

facts.label: Over complex numbers
facts.value: Every denominator piece has degree one, with constant numerators

facts.label: Over real numbers
facts.value: Some denominator pieces may be quadratic

facts.label: Residues
facts.value: Coefficients of the 1/(x − α_j) terms are called residues

items.prompt: A fraction of polynomials has a numerator of higher degree than its denominator. What is the first move?

options.label: Divide the top by the bottom with polynomial long division
Split the denominator into pieces straight away
Multiply both top and bottom by the denominator
Cancel the highest power from both

items.explain: If the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's, do the Euclidean division using polynomial long division, then seek partial fractions for the remainder fraction.

items.prompt: A calculus student must find the antiderivative of a fraction of two polynomials. How does decomposition help?

options.label: It turns the fraction into a single simple term
It splits it into a polynomial plus fractions with simpler denominators
It removes the denominator completely
It only checks whether an answer exists

items.explain: The decomposition writes the fraction as a polynomial plus fractions with simpler denominators, which provides an algorithm for explicit antiderivatives.

items.prompt: A denominator has a factor that cannot be broken down further over the given field and is not of degree one. What must the numerator over that factor look like?

options.label: A constant, as for every other piece
Any polynomial, with no limit on its degree
A polynomial of the same degree as the factor
A polynomial of smaller degree than the factor, not just a constant

items.explain: Each numerator is a polynomial of smaller degree than the irreducible polynomial in its denominator, so over a factor that is not of degree one it need not be a constant.

items.prompt: A program decomposes a fraction whose coefficients are whole numbers. Why might it use square-free factorization rather than full irreducible factorization?

options.label: It is much easier to compute and avoids bringing in irrational coefficients
It always gives fewer terms than the finer decomposition does
It works only when every denominator piece has degree one
It lets the program skip the Euclidean division step entirely

items.explain: Replacing irreducible by square-free polynomials swaps factorization for a much easier computation. It is enough for most uses and avoids irrational coefficients when the inputs are integers or rationals.

items.prompt: You have written unknown numerators over each simpler denominator. How do you find them?

options.label: Guess whole numbers until the sides agree
Put the pieces over a common denominator and equate coefficients of each power of x
Ignore the denominators and compare numerators one at a time
Differentiate both sides until the unknowns disappear

items.explain: Reducing the sum to a common denominator and equating the coefficients of each power of x gives a system of linear equations for the unknown coefficients.

items.prompt: Working over the complex numbers, what does the fundamental theorem of algebra imply about the pieces?

options.label: Every denominator has degree one and every numerator is a constant
Every numerator is zero and the denominators multiply
Denominators may be quadratic, with linear numerators
The decomposition no longer exists

items.explain: Over the complex numbers, the fundamental theorem of algebra implies that all denominator pieces have degree one and all numerators are constants.
